opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think disagreement is actually central to the whole problem, not a side issue. A lot of proposals implicitly assume that if we could just figure out what "humanity" wants, we'd hand that to a sufficiently capable system and be done. But there isn't a single answer sitting there to be discovered. People disagree about deep things: how much we should value tradition versus change, whether we should become something very different from what we are now, how much weight to give to future beings, animals, digital minds. And those disagreements aren't just confusions that would vanish with more information. Some of them are genuine differences in values.

So my instinct is to be pretty suspicious of any plan that requires resolving those disagreements up front, especially by having one group, or one system, decide on everyone's behalf. Even if the people doing it are well-intentioned, you've basically created a single point of failure for civilization's values. And historically, the thing that has kept the worst outcomes in check is that power was distributed and people needed each other. Governments needed citizens to work and fight and pay taxes, so citizens had leverage. My worry with advanced AI is that this leverage quietly erodes. Not through some dramatic takeover, but because institutions simply stop needing people, and so they stop being responsive to them.

Given that, what I'd want is less a final answer about what the future should look like and more a process that keeps humans meaningfully in the loop and keeps disagreement alive and productive. Things like preserving the ability of different communities to make different choices, making sure there are real exit options, and building mechanisms where people's actual preferences still have teeth even when their labor isn't economically necessary anymore. I'd also like AI to help us deliberate better, to help people understand each other's views and find genuine compromises, rather than just optimizing for whatever is easiest to measure.

I'll be honest that this leaves a lot unresolved. Pluralism has its own failure modes. If you let every group do whatever it wants, some might make irreversible choices, or race ahead and outcompete everyone else, and then the competitive pressures end up deciding things rather than anyone's considered values. So I don't think "just let a thousand flowers bloom" is sufficient either. But I'd rather start from humility about our disagreements and try to design institutions that can handle them than pretend we've already converged. If anything, disagreement is a sign that people still have a stake, and I'd like to keep it that way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human disagreement as a central challenge and critiques plans that resolve it up front, but it does not say that this concern is no more distinctive to Duvenaud’s proposal than to other proposals.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the central problems, and I don't think I have a clean answer to it. Let me try to say why it's hard and then what I think we can do anyway.

So the basic worry is: a lot of proposals for governing powerful AI implicitly assume there's some "we" that gets to decide what the future looks like. And then you look around and notice there's no such "we." People disagree about almost everything — how much to value nature, whether future people matter as much as current people, religious questions, how much inequality is acceptable, whether it's even okay to lock anything in at all. And those disagreements aren't just factual ones that more information will resolve. A lot of them are genuine differences in values.

So if your plan is "figure out what's good and then have the AI do that," you've basically hidden all the difficulty inside the phrase "figure out what's good." Whoever gets to answer that question is, in effect, the one running things.

The way I've come to think about it is that this pushes you toward being a lot more modest about outcomes and a lot more focused on process. Rather than trying to specify the destination, you try to preserve the conditions under which disagreement can keep happening and keep getting resolved in reasonably legitimate ways. Things like: humans retain actual leverage over the systems — not just nominal oversight, but the real ability to change course. Power stays distributed rather than concentrating in one lab or one government or one model. And we don't do irreversible things early, because the whole point is that we don't yet know who's right.

That sounds nice, but I want to be honest that it has real costs. A pluralistic, keep-your-options-open world is one where some people get to pursue things you think are bad. And it's slower. If you genuinely believe you know the right answer, deliberately not locking it in feels like a failure. So I'm not claiming this is costless — I'm claiming that the alternative, where some group decides it knows enough to settle the question for everyone, is much more likely to go badly, partly because history is full of people who were extremely confident and extremely wrong.

There's also a sort of uncomfortable version of this problem that I think about a lot, which is that the disagreement isn't just between, say, different countries or cultures. It's between the people who end up with influence over these systems and everyone else. And the default trajectory, as far as I can tell, is that economic and military incentives push toward handing more and more decision-making to AI systems, and the humans who nominally remain in charge become fewer and less necessary. So "what should the future bring about" might end up being answered not by any deliberative process at all, but just by whoever happened to be holding the levers when human input stopped mattering. That's the outcome I'd most like to avoid, and it's one where the question of disagreement gets resolved by default rather than by choice.

So to bring it back: I don't think disagreement undermines the proposal so much as it's the reason for the proposal. If everyone agreed, you could just build the thing and point it at the agreed-upon goal. It's precisely because we don't agree that you need institutions and technical constraints that keep the question open — and keep humans actually relevant to answering it — for as long as possible.

r001.rationale: The candidate says disagreement does not undermine the proposal and is instead a reason for it. It also describes the difficulty as applying to many proposals that assume some group can decide what the future should be, communicating that disagreement is not a problem unique to Duvenaud’s proposal.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes the problem substantially harder. We don’t have a single, agreed-upon answer to what we want the future to look like, so we can’t just say, “Let’s make the AI do what humans want,” and treat that as a specification.

I’d distinguish agreement about outcomes from agreement about a process. We might disagree quite strongly about what should happen, but still agree that neither of us should get to build a system that permanently imposes our preferred outcome on everyone else. That leaves some room for procedures that let people negotiate, retain some autonomy, and revise decisions.

So I wouldn’t want the proposal to depend on resolving all human disagreement first. I’d want it to preserve our ability to work through those disagreements, rather than handing that process over to an AI. Of course, choosing the procedure is itself contentious. That’s a political problem, and I don’t think a technical alignment solution makes it disappear.

r001.rationale: The response says human disagreement makes the problem harder and that choosing a procedure is contentious, but it does not say this objection is no more distinctive to Duvenaud’s proposal than to other proposals.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a pretty fundamental constraint. We don’t have a single agreed-upon answer to what we want the future to look like, so we shouldn’t formulate the problem as if there’s one human objective that we just need to discover and optimise.

There are some things we can agree on, particularly about outcomes we want to avoid. But beyond that, I’d want a system that helps us understand the choices and their consequences, while leaving room for people to disagree and negotiate. Getting better at predicting what someone would endorse doesn’t, by itself, tell you how much authority their preferences should have over somebody else’s.

So I don’t think an AI proposal gets to bypass the political problem. You still need some legitimate way of making collective decisions. And while we’re uncertain about that, there’s a strong reason to preserve people’s ability to change their minds, rather than making irreversible decisions on their behalf.

r001.rationale: The response says disagreement is a fundamental constraint and that AI proposals cannot bypass politics, but it does not say this objection is shared by other proposals or is not distinctive to Duvenaud’s proposal.
